title: AQA GCSE English Language: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
description: Common AQA GCSE English Language mistakes in reading and writing answers, with practical fixes for analysis, structure, evaluation, comparison and Question 5.

children: AQA GCSE English Language: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
Reading Mistakes That Cost Marks

Many weaker answers are not caused by a lack of ideas. They come from using the wrong evidence, answering a slightly different question, naming a technique without analysing it or writing generic comments that could apply to almost any text.
Feature spotting:
naming metaphor, simile or personification without explaining the specific word choice and its effect.
Oversized quotations:
copying whole sentences when one or two precise words would produce more focused analysis.
Generic reader effects:
writing ‘this makes the reader want to read on’ instead of explaining the particular impression or idea created.
Ignoring the line range:
using evidence from outside the section named in the question.
Answering from memory:
relying on a rehearsed formula instead of adapting the response to the actual extract and wording.

A useful correction routine is: identify the exact mistake, rewrite only the weak sentence or paragraph, then test the same skill on a fresh extract. That is more effective than simply reading a model answer and moving on.

Revision Mistakes That Create the Illusion of Progress

English Language revision needs output. Reading notes and watching explanations can help, but improvement becomes visible when you produce an answer, receive feedback and then apply that feedback to another task.
Only rereading notes:
turn notes into a question, paragraph or retrieval task so you have to produce something.
Doing full papers too early:
isolate weak questions first, then combine them into timed sections once the methods are secure.
Checking the mark but not the cause:
record why marks were lost, not just the final score.
Never rewriting weak work:
correct a poor paragraph while the feedback is still fresh.
Practising only favourite tasks:
allocate more time to the question types that consistently underperform.
Ignoring timing until the exam:
add realistic time limits gradually after the underlying skill is secure.
Collecting resources instead of using them:
a smaller number of marked, corrected tasks is usually more informative than dozens of untouched worksheets.

A revision session should leave behind evidence: a paragraph, a plan, an annotated extract, a corrected answer or a short timed response. If there is nothing to evaluate, it is difficult to know whether the skill improved.
Question-Specific Mistakes

Different AQA questions reward different skills. A strong method for one question can become a poor method when copied mechanically into another, so revise the purpose of each question rather than relying on one universal paragraph formula.
Paper 1 Question 2:
do not turn language analysis into a hunt for named techniques; analyse the writer’s precise choices and effects.
Paper 1 Question 3: analyse structure, sequence and shifts in focus across the source, linking them to the specific effect named in the current question rather than discussing only language.
do not discuss only language when the focus is structure, sequence, focus and how the text is organised.
Paper 1 Question 4:
make a clear evaluation and support it with analysis rather than simply agreeing with the statement.
Paper 2 Question 4:
compare viewpoints and how they are conveyed; two separate analyses with no direct comparison weaken the response.
Use the Paper 1 and Paper 2 guides alongside this checklist when you need the exact mark allocation and assessment focus for an individual question.

Writing Mistakes in Question 5

The 40-mark writing task rewards content and organisation as well as technical accuracy. A response can contain impressive vocabulary and still underperform if the viewpoint, structure or control of sentences is weak.
No clear purpose:
decide what you want the reader to think, feel or understand before writing.
Overcomplicated plot or argument:
control a smaller number of ideas rather than introducing more than you can develop.
Device stuffing:
use rhetorical or descriptive techniques because they serve the piece, not because they appear on a checklist.
Uncontrolled punctuation:
ambitious punctuation only helps when sentence boundaries remain secure.
Paragraph drift:
make each paragraph do a deliberate job in the overall structure.
No proofreading:
reserve time to check spelling, agreement, missing words and punctuation errors that can be corrected quickly.
After writing, do not ask only whether it sounds impressive. Check whether the piece is clear, shaped for the task, controlled at sentence level and deliberately organised from beginning to end.
Turn Marking Into the Next Revision Task

The value of feedback depends on what you do with it. A page of comments has little effect if the next piece of work repeats the same weakness. Convert feedback into one or two observable actions that can be checked in the next response.
Use the official assessment focus:
check what the question is actually rewarding before deciding how to improve it.
Keep an error log:
group repeated weaknesses such as vague analysis, weak evidence selection or sentence-boundary errors.
Choose one priority:
turn a broad comment such as ‘analyse more’ into a specific action you can perform next time.
Rewrite the weak section:
apply the feedback immediately rather than merely reading it.
Test the change on new material:
improvement is more convincing when the better method transfers to a different extract or task.

The strongest revision loop is simple: attempt, diagnose, correct, repeat. Over time, your error log should show fewer repeated problems and more independent control of the skills that previously needed prompting.

Avoid trying to fix every weakness at once. Choose the error that is costing the most marks, practise it deliberately and then retest it.
